QUERY LIST

Use the Queries header destination or /ql. This list contains only the
current server's private conversations. The query name remains on the
conversation row and never replaces a header category.

Up/Down or k/j selects a query row. Left/Right or h/l chooses its action
beneath the heading and Enter executes it; Open is selected initially.
Horizontal arrows
stay within this list, including when it is empty. In an empty list, Open on
the New query... row opens Command with /pm prepared. The selected row and
action are highlighted together, and changing the row preserves the action.
Available actions:

    Open    New    Close    Back

Up/Down stops at the first/last row. New opens Command with /pm prepared
and preserves the existing chat draft. Close removes the selected query;
a nonempty draft requires confirmation, defaulting to No. Back or Escape
returns to main chat editing.

Home/End or g/G selects endpoints. Direct aliases are c for Close and o or
n for New. Mouse item clicks open a query; action-row clicks act on the
selected item. Narrow action bars keep the focused action visible with side
arrows.

/pm NICK|NUMBER opens or selects a query without sending anything, even
disconnected.
Chat editing is ready immediately afterward. Escape from the query opens
Queries with that query selected, including when it was opened by a command,
mouse action, or activity entry. Escape from Queries restores the query
and its draft. /msg NICK TEXT sends directly.
Close a private view by nickname with /close NICK.

MENTIONS AND WATCH STRINGS

Your current nickname is watched automatically. Nickname matching follows
the IRC server's advertised case mapping and nickname boundaries. A nickname
change updates this automatic match.

    /watch add project name
    /watch remove project name
    /watch list

Custom watch values are literal substrings, not regular expressions or
shell patterns. IRC/ASCII letter and symbol case rules are used; non-ASCII
characters match exactly. Up to 32 custom values of 127 UTF-8 bytes each
are accepted. Use /save during normal operation to preserve changes in the
selected configuration. In test mode, changes remain in memory.
Mentions are retained in memory, subject to the history limits. They are
not a permanent notification archive or an on-disk log.
Timestamps are local receipt dates and times, in YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS form.

CONVERSATION COMMANDS

    /join CHANNEL [KEY]     request to join one channel, optionally with a key
    /part [CHANNEL] [MESSAGE] leave a channel with an optional PART reason
    /close [NAME|NUMBER]   close a channel/query; number is a channel number
    /pm NICK|NUMBER               open/switch a private view without sending
    text
    /msg TARGET TEXT       send text to one nickname or channel
    /me TEXT               send an IRC action to the current conversation
    /nick NICK             request a different nickname
    /away [MESSAGE]        set away with text; without text, clear away
    /back                  clear away status; takes no argument
    /whois NICK            request information about a nickname
    /topic                 request the current channel topic
    /topic TEXT            request a new current-channel topic
    /connect [HOST [PORT]] connect directly, or reuse the selected server
    /disconnect [NUMBER] disconnect this or a numbered server; retain
    views/drafts
    /dcc or /transfers     open the shared File transfers screen
    /cancel               stop unsent chat messages on this server
    /background           keep running and return to the shell
    /quit [MESSAGE]       exit all server sessions with an optional QUIT reason
    /settings             edit app-wide preferences and any server profile
    /save [input|output|all] save selected, primary, or all profiles
    /saveconf             save profiles and remember the selected connection
    /set autoconnect on    enable connection at future startup after saving
    /set autoconnect off   disable it

/away MESSAGE sends one standard AWAY message. Text is limited to the
current wire limit minus 8 bytes (504 bytes at the usual 512-byte limit);
oversized text or controls are rejected, never split. /away with no text
and /back clear away. These require registration. The indicator changes
only on server acknowledgments and resets on disconnect/reconnect.
The server list's Away action sends Away as the message or clears an
acknowledged away state, preserving the view and draft. A disconnected
server must connect first. Edit ignored senders in the Settings Ignore
fields, or use the local /ignore and /unignore commands.

/join accepts one channel and at most one key token. Keys must be printable
ASCII without spaces, colon, or comma, and the complete JOIN must fit the
wire limit. The key is not logged or saved; only the channel name enters
auto-join. Re-enter the key when needed after reconnecting or restarting.
The offline simulator acknowledges away changes and accepts transient
join keys, but does not test a real channel's key or admission policy.

The server decides permissions, nickname availability, channel admission,
and whether topic changes are allowed. Local command acceptance does not
guarantee server acceptance or delivery to another participant.
Messages you submit wait briefly while vipirc sends chat lines at least
1.2 seconds apart. /cancel removes those still waiting on the selected
server, across its channels and queries. It does not erase your draft or
recall text already sent. A message already being transmitted may finish.
/join and /part update the auto-join selection; /save
preserves that selection for future launches unless pending Settings startup
choices override it.
/part also discards queued text for that channel while retaining the view
and its history. A message already in flight may finish before PART. Text after
the channel is the PART reason; when the channel is omitted, text is the reason
for the selected channel. With no explicit reason, [presence] part_message is
used. Closing a joined channel uses the same default PART reason.

/quit MESSAGE uses that text as the best-effort IRC QUIT reason on live server
sessions. Without text, [presence] quit_message is used; an empty default sends
a bare QUIT. Shutdown remains bounded and never waits indefinitely for a dead
network.

Automatic away status is separate from manual /away. With background_away on,
a successful Background action or managed terminal loss queues the configured
AWAY only after the terminal has detached. Resuming clears only that automatic
status. autoaway_minutes applies the same rule after local input inactivity;
zero disables the idle timer. Any manual /away remains set until /back or an
explicit /away with no message. Incoming IRC traffic never counts as local user
activity.

LOCAL IGNORE FILTERS

    /ignore or /ignore list       list masks in the server view
    /ignore MASK                 add a mask; /ignore add MASK also works
    /unignore MASK               remove it; /ignore remove MASK also works
    /ignore clear                remove all masks

These local commands work disconnected. Use /ignore add NICK for nicknames
literally named list, add, remove, or clear. Up to 32 masks of 127 ASCII
bytes each are accepted. A plain mask must be an exact valid nickname.
Wildcards require full nick!user@host form with three nonempty components;
for example, *!*@*.example. Within each component, * matches zero or more
bytes and ? matches one byte. Other permitted bytes are literal; there are
no regex classes, escaping, or shell expansion. Nick uses IRC case rules;
user and host ignore ASCII case. Whitespace, controls, and non-ASCII are
invalid.
Removal compares stored patterns under those case rules; it does not expand
wildcards to remove other masks.

Only incoming user-originated PRIVMSG/NOTICE is filtered, before mentions
or query creation. A source needs an explicit user prefix; nickname-only
masks can match incomplete user/host details, while full masks require all
three parts. Bare server notices and all protocol/membership state remain
visible. Existing history is retained. Filtering is local, not a server ban.
Settings edits the same list; Apply acts live. /save or Settings Save persists
it in normal mode; test-mode edits stay in memory. Config repeats mask= in
[ignore].

DELAYED STARTUP COMMANDS

    /autocommands list
    /autocommands add /msg NickServ IDENTIFY account <password>
    /autocommands add /msg ChanServ OP #room mynick
    /autocommands delay 15
    /autocommands interval 2
    /autocommands remove 1
    /autocommands on
    /autocommands off
    /autocommands clear
    /save

Each server has its own list of at most 16 literal single-line commands,
at most 511 UTF-8 bytes each. Allowed commands are /msg TARGET TEXT,
/join #channel [key], /nick NICK, /away [TEXT], /back, and /whois NICK.
The exact aliases /message, /privmsg, /j, /nickname and /unaway also work.
No shell, raw protocol command, variable expansion, or implicit current chat
target is available. Prefer SASL through /autoauth for account authentication
when the network supports it.

The sequence starts once per successful connection, after registration and
required SASL. The default initial delay is 15 seconds (allowed 0..300).
Each later command waits two seconds after the previous write completes
(allowed 2..60). Only one automatic command is queued or in flight at a time;
a stalled connection never produces a catch-up burst. Automatic messages
must fit one IRC message and are not split, locally echoed, or retained in
command history. They do not open query windows. Replies from services arrive
normally. Automatic JOIN acknowledgments do not switch the selected chat.

Edits are staged for the next connection. /cancel stops the current pending
sequence and queued chat; it does not recall transmitted bytes or interrupt
an in-flight TLS retry. Closing or parting a target cancels a remaining
sequence that refers to it. A failure cancels later commands and identifies
the failed position without printing command text. Reconnecting begins a new
sequence; offline test mode never runs one.

Enabled nonempty lists require verified TLS. Every configuration with a
nonempty list, even when disabled, must be an owned regular 0600/0400 file.
Commands may contain passwords. /autocommands list hides message/key text.
New server profiles start with no commands; changing a destination clears an
unchanged inherited list. Save explicitly to keep edits.

    [autocommands]
    enabled=true
    delay_seconds=15
    interval_seconds=2
    command=/msg ChanServ OP #room mynick

Repeated command= lines retain order. Bytes after '=' are literal, including
trailing spaces, '#', ';' and additional '='. Lines are never shell commands.

PROGRAM AND QUEUE NOTIFICATIONS, QUERY NUMBERS, AND ALIASES

/set queue_notices off hides routine queued/paced acknowledgments in all
interfaces and servers. /set queue_notices on restores them. In the minimalist
frontend, an explicitly reviewed send omits its redundant routine queue
acknowledgment even when queue notices are enabled.
/set program_messages off separately hides low-priority local feedback such as
draft-cancelled, input-cleared, preserved-draft, and similar success/cancel
notices. Errors, byte-limit warnings, and send confirmations remain visible.
Both defaults are true. /save output or /saveconf persists the global [output]
settings. The same preferences appear in /panel Application preferences and
graphical Interface settings.

/ql numbers private queries separately, starting at 1. /query 2 or /pm 2
selects its second entry; a nickname works in the same argument. Closing a
query renumbers later entries. Opening a query sends no message. Channel 0
still opens the server's messages and MOTD.

Common exact aliases include /j, /leave, /message, /privmsg, /nickname,
/names, /nicks, /conn, /disc, /unaway, /detach, /saveconfig, /configure and
/preferences. They share command validation, completion and privacy rules.
Unknown spellings remain errors rather than guessing an action to execute.

Membership changes, MOTD, WHOIS, invites and common errors use readable
messages with useful server detail. Internal identity/capability replies do
not add duplicate protocol bookkeeping to the chat display. Unknown replies
retain the server's text without treating a numeric code as the explanation.

FILE TRANSFERS

The File transfers header destination, /dcc, and /transfers open the same
global
transfer screen. Records identify their originating IRC server. Up/Down
selects a transfer; Left/Right selects an action; Enter executes it:

    Accept    Reject    Send...    Cancel transfer    Back

Alongside arrows, j/k selects rows, h/l selects actions, and g/G selects
endpoints. Mouse
rows select records and action clicks execute the selected action. The
screen needs at least 12 rows by 20 columns for transfer review. Escape from
a file browser or field editor returns to its form; Escape from the form or
transfer list restores main chat without discarding drafts or stopping
accepted transfers. F1..F6 open available global destinations.

This release supports active classic IPv4 DCC SEND only. It does not support
DCC CHAT, resume, passive/reverse transfers, automatic acceptance, automatic
address discovery, or automatic port forwarding. A transfer can contain at
most 4,294,967,295 bytes. Received files are never opened or executed for you.

DCC transfers are unencrypted direct peer connections, independent of IRC
TLS. The protocol does not cryptographically authenticate a connecting peer.
An outgoing offer discloses its advertised IPv4; accepting an offer reveals
the receiving host's IP to the peer. Check the sender, intended file, byte
size, and displayed endpoint before approving each transfer.

Receiving

An incoming offer is stored without opening any file or socket. Reject
refuses it without creating either. Accept in the list opens a review form
with Directory and Save as fields and these actions below the heading:

    Edit    Accept    Cancel

Review the peer endpoint and size, edit the destination if needed, then
choose the form's Accept to start. Enter in a field stages it; it does not
accept the offer. Cancel returns to the list. Field paste inserts data only;
unsupported controls cannot commit it. Paste outside a field is ignored.

The default directory is $XDG_DATA_HOME/vipirc/downloads when XDG_DATA_HOME
is absolute, otherwise $HOME/.local/share/vipirc/downloads when HOME is
absolute. Without an absolute base, enter a destination explicitly. Missing
destination ancestors are created with mode 0700 only after Accept. The
final directory must be private and owned by you. A new regular file uses
mode 0600; existing files, symlinks, and '..' paths are refused.

The offered or chosen basename must be visible and nonhidden, with no path
separators, control/bidirectional-formatting characters, or quotes. Quoted
wire filenames may contain internal spaces. Failed or cancelled partial
files are removed only if they still identify the file created for that
transfer; a replacement file is not removed.

Sending

Select Send... to open a form containing Nickname, Source file, Advertised
IPv4, and Listen port. A current query supplies its nickname as a default.
The form names the IRC server through which the offer will be sent. Its
actions sit below the heading: Edit (Browse for Source file), Offer, Cancel.
Offer explicitly starts the listener and
queues the offer through that registered server's paced chat path.

Activate Source file to open the file browser at the launch directory.
Up/Down selects a row; Enter opens a directory or chooses a regular file.
The parent entry or Backspace moves up. Type path accepts a direct absolute
filename. Escape cancels the browser without changing the source field.
Choosing a file fills the form; it does not offer or transmit it. The browser
never changes the process working directory. It reads at most 64 directory
entries per event-loop step, retains at most 512 entries, and stops after
4096 examined entries, reporting a limit when reached. Use Type path when a
needed file is outside that bounded listing. Symlinks and unsafe names are
omitted; metadata is checked again when selecting and offering the file.

Source file must identify an existing regular file; symlinks and '..'
components are refused. Enter the IPv4 address the
receiver can reach. Listen port 0 chooses an available local port; an
explicit value is from 1 through 65535. Behind NAT, use the appropriate
advertised address and a forwarded port. vipirc does not discover the
public address, configure UPnP, or arrange forwarding.

With SSH, all paths, HOME/XDG download directories, listening/advertised
addresses, and peer connections belong to the host running vipirc. That
may be the remote SSH host. The terminal emulator's local filesystem and
network address are not used for these transfers.

Commands in either interface

    /dcc alice file.txt
    /dcc send -address 203.0.113.10 -port 5000 alice file with spaces.txt
    /dcc list
    /dcc accept 1 /home/me/private-downloads
    /dcc reject 2
    /dcc cancel 3

The example address must be replaced with a reachable address. Relative paths
refer to the directory where vipirc was launched, including in -i mode.
The source path is the literal remainder after the nickname, including spaces;
do not add shell quotes or escaping. If no advertised address is supplied,
the command uses the IRC socket's local IPv4 address; an IPv6-only connection
needs an explicit IPv4 address, and NAT may require an override and
forwarding.
The command does not discover a public address or change networking rules.

The optional receive directory defaults to the launch directory and must
pass the same private-directory checks. No file is created before explicit
Accept. Bare /dcc opens the graphical list or prints the minimalist list.
Both interfaces share the transfer manager, limits, cancel behavior and
offline prohibition on file/socket access for Send or Accept.

Lifecycle and bounds

Accepted transfers continue while chatting, switching servers, or
Disconnecting IRC. Cancel transfer stops one transfer. Closing its server
cancels that server's offers and transfers; quitting stops all of them.
Cancellation, failure, or expiry also removes a still-queued outgoing
offer. An offer already sent or in flight cannot be recalled.

The workspace permits eight pending offers, four active/listening/connecting
transfers, and twelve retained transfer records in total. Completed or failed
records are recycled oldest-first only when full; transfer IDs are not
reused during a run. Pending offers expire after five minutes. Transfers
stop after two minutes without progress. File data is streamed in bounded
buffers, with cumulative 32-bit acknowledgments.

In --test-mode a memory-only sample offer permits list/reject/cancel review.
Send and Accept are disabled before any filesystem or socket access. Real
file transfers require restarting without --test-mode.

INPUT EDITING

These keys apply while editing the main chat draft:

    Enter                  send or review the composed text
    Left                   previous character group
    Right                  next character group
    Up / Down              move between wrapped visual input rows
    Home                   beginning of the complete composition
    End                    end of the complete composition
    Backspace              remove the previous character group
    Delete                 remove the character group under the caret
    Tab / Shift-Tab        complete next / previous matching nickname
    Esc                    open vipirc; ordinary panels return to chat

F1 through F6 open the available category panels. Escape from Settings
returns to vipirc. Up at the first wrapped input row stays in the editor.

Typed Enter or Send below the field submits; explicit newlines can be
composed through bracketed chat paste. Pasted tabs become spaces without
changing focus. /clearinput or Clear below the field clears the entire
draft, including offscreen text, without changing input focus. Clearing
never sends text and requires no preliminary select-all step. A typed slash
at caret position zero opens Command while preserving this draft; a slash
later in the line or any pasted slash remains ordinary chat text.

The composition is a flat logical buffer. Screen wrapping does not insert
characters. Backspace at the beginning of a wrapped row removes the last
character of the preceding row. Resizing the terminal retains the text and
cursor position.

Input height is fixed for the current view and its protocol byte budget.
For B ordinary-message payload bytes and W usable terminal columns, it
reserves floor(B/W)+1 rows, including the caret cell. The border occupies
the outer columns; W is the space inside it. A budget of 465 bytes at 99
usable columns reserves five rows. Small terminals clamp the height to
available rows. Views without a chat recipient use a one-character recipient
allowance when calculating their height.

Typing and deleting do not grow or shrink the chat field. Longer drafts
scroll within it to keep the caret visible. Command has its own fixed editor;
opening or running /msg or /me does not resize or replace the chat draft. A
terminal
resize, view switch, or actual protocol-budget change recalculates the
height. The draft and cursor position remain intact.

An isolated raw Escape waits about 500 ms to distinguish it from the start
of a terminal sequence. A sequence already in progress allows 1,000 ms
between continuation bytes. Networking continues during these waits;
complete keys decoded by curses are handled immediately.

Opening paste markers must arrive within these timing windows. If the first
Escape is left alone past its grace period, it acts as Escape; in the
vipirc -i log, that can exit the program. Once paste capture starts, closing
markers remain recognized across arbitrarily delayed, split reads.

UTF-8 is used for input and messages. Set a UTF-8 locale so the terminal and
the curses library agree about display widths. ASCII is already its
one-byte subset; no manual encoding switch is needed. SSH does not
change the encoded message length. On each remote host, inspect the session:

    locale
    locale charmap
    locale -a

The first two show locale settings and character encoding; locale -a lists
installed locales. The effective LC_CTYPE on the host running vipirc should
use an installed UTF-8 locale matching the terminal. Names vary across
systems, so check each SSH host. TERM identifies terminal capabilities,
not encoding. The client does not guess terminal encoding or transcode
legacy character sets.

The active LC_CTYPE is respected. A UTF-8 locale enables Unicode editing.
A non-UTF-8 or invalid locale selects ASCII terminal mode. The welcome
screen explains the mode. ASCII
typing works; non-ASCII input is refused with a clear status message.
Incoming non-ASCII code points display as '?' without changing the stored
network text. The client does not force a locale or change terminal
settings. Select an installed UTF-8 locale and restart for Unicode use.

A base character and its following zero-width marks move and delete
together. Full Unicode grapheme segmentation, including indivisible
multi-character emoji sequences, is not implemented. Unsupported glyphs
receive a visible replacement where needed.

The composition accepts up to 8,192 Unicode scalar values and 16,384 UTF-8
bytes. These are draft-storage bounds; the much smaller message budget
below determines warnings and splitting. The first storage limit reached
applies. Invalid UTF-8 and terminal controls are rejected. Pasted newlines
remain visible in the composition and are considered when calculating how
many IRC messages would be needed.

MOUSE CONTROLS

Mouse controls are enabled by default when curses and the terminal support
mouse events. /mouse toggles the preference; /mouse on or /mouse off sets it.
Settings > Interface > Mouse edits the same value. The configuration key is
[interface]
mouse=true or mouse=false. To retain this app-wide preference, use Settings >
Interface > Save, or /save while the primary server is selected. /save on a
secondary server writes only that server's profile; its legacy mouse value
does not override the primary preference at startup. The same persistence
rule applies to the app-wide User list preference.

Click a global header category to open it. The conversation identity below
the header is a label, not a substitute for the Servers or Channels control.
Click inside the chat-field border to place the caret and type. Clear below
the field erases the entire draft without changing input focus. Send follows
the same validation, length warning, and split confirmation as typed Enter.
Clear/Send are hidden when mouse handling is off or unavailable. Enter and
/clearinput remain usable. Clicking a nickname in chat or the roster opens
its context menu, including Whois and Query. Clicking a #channel joins it
if necessary or switches to its existing joined view. The displayed token,
not a later replacement at the same coordinates, determines the action.

A server/channel/query item click opens the item; a click on the action
row beneath the heading acts on the selected item. The wheel changes row
selection while preserving the selected
action. Both selections stay highlighted. Back or Escape returns to main
chat. Settings and transfer screens retain their own field and action
controls.

Over conversation history, each wheel step scrolls three visual rows; over
the user roster it scrolls three users. The main chat display needs at least
9 rows and 20 columns. The global header and conversation row sit above
history, the fixed chat field, and the conditional Clear/Send controls.
Empty header categories are omitted; counts appear in parentheses for
categories with
content. A narrow header keeps the selected destination visible.

The terminal and any SSH multiplexer must forward mouse events. Availability
depends on curses, TERM, and the terminal; keyboard operation remains usable.
Mouse clicks do not acknowledge the early length popup or multi-message
confirmation. Those require their displayed keyboard choices. Mouse handling
does not open URLs or transfer clipboard text.

Command has explicit Run and Cancel controls. A pasted click sequence or
pasted newline cannot activate them. Enter/Run must be a fresh action after
the paste has ended. Clicks from a previous screen layout are not reused as
actions on a newly opened screen.

MESSAGE LENGTH AND FLOOD PREVENTION

Ordinary IRC protocol lines are limited to 512 bytes, including CR and LF.
That is a wire-line limit, not a limit of 512 user-visible characters.
ASCII uses one byte per character. A Unicode code point uses one to four
UTF-8 bytes, and a displayed glyph can contain multiple code points.
Command, destination, and relay prefix also take space. For a relayed
message of the form

    :nick!user@host PRIVMSG target :text<CR><LF>

the budget used by vipirc is

    B = L - (len(nick) + len(user) + len(host)
             + len(target) + len("PRIVMSG") + 9)

L is normally 512, reduced by a recognized smaller server LINELEN value.
Lengths in this expression are bytes. IRC actions have an additional
envelope, whose bytes are also subtracted. Until the full relay identity is
known, conservative identity allowances reduce B. Different destinations
and identity changes can therefore change the current payload budget.

In the full curses interface, a popup appears as soon as the longest logical
payload line reaches B bytes, or the draft already needs multiple messages:

    Message limit reached (B bytes).
    More text will need multiple chat lines.
    Enter/Esc: keep editing. Nothing sent.

If the draft already needs multiple messages, the middle line instead says
"This draft needs multiple chat lines." Enter or Esc returns to Input mode;
neither sends the draft. Other keys cannot dismiss the popup, and a short
key-repeat guard protects acknowledgment. The warning is shown once per
threshold crossing.

In vipirc -i, the same computed boundary is pre-emptive. Its editor shows:

    Message limit reached (B bytes). Enter confirms continued editing; Backspace/Delete can reduce; Esc cancels.

Until Enter acknowledges that boundary, further text insertion is blocked.
That Enter only authorizes continued editing; it sends nothing. Editing back
below one message rearms the warning. Once an acknowledged draft needs several
IRC messages, the editor states that split transmission still requires
separate explicit confirmation. /msg, /me, and // are measured by their actual
outgoing payload; unrelated local commands do not trigger the warning.
Bracketed paste is checked after the paste finishes and remains intact within
the input bounds.

When Enter submits a composition needing more than one message, the client
presents a separate send confirmation:

    This text needs N IRC messages. Send all? [y/N]

Enter or n declines. Sending requires an affirmative y. Splits occur only
between complete UTF-8 characters, with nonempty message text preserved.
Explicit newlines separate messages; empty lines are skipped. No split is
sent before confirmation. Local slash commands must remain single-line;
compose multiline chat in the selected conversation instead.
Accepted chat messages are paced at least 1.2 seconds apart; the bounded
send queue holds at most 64 messages. Server flood rules can be stricter.
Protocol control traffic such as PONG is handled separately from chat.

The network can impose additional rules or reject messages. vipirc keeps
the ordinary 512-byte compatibility ceiling; it does not assume that a
server will accept a larger line merely because an extension exists.

profile and its adjacent catalog of saved secondary profiles. Up to eight

    port=6697
    tls=true
    nick=tutankh-aten
    username=

    channel=#ircnow

    auth_user=

    server_password_file=
    server_password_gpg_file=

    ca_file=

    hints=true

The nickname and IRC username are different fields. An empty nickname is
prompted at interactive startup. The username defaults from your Unix
account. realname is the descriptive IRC USER field; it need not be your
legal name. channel is a comma-separated auto-join list, without spaces.
An empty channel value leaves you in the server view.

program_messages controls low-priority feedback; queue_notices separately
controls pacing notices. Errors and required confirmations remain visible.
Persistent logging is off by default. When enabled, each saved profile appends
to CONFIG_PATH.log in an owned directory with exact mode 0700. All symlink
components are refused, and the opened file must be owned, single-link,
regular, and exactly mode 0600. A FIFO cannot block the open.

Each log has a 16 MiB limit protected by a nonblocking write lock. Reaching the
limit, encountering an unsafe path, or a write/lock failure stops logging for
that profile and reports an error; live chat continues. Existing data is never
automatically removed. Archive the log, then toggle logging off/on to resume.
Regular files on slow storage can still delay disk I/O. Logs survive exit.
Known outgoing service/credential commands and incoming service replies are
excluded. Unsent drafts and SASL/PASS buffers are not supplied to the logger.
Custom service identities and ordinary chat can still contain secrets.

single_session is false by default. When true, the client refuses creation of a
second background job in its local vipirc namespace. It does not reduce the
eight-server capacity of the one live session; it only makes the local resume
job count singular.

Presence preferences are application-wide. part_message defaults to empty;
quit_message defaults to Client quit. background_away defaults on with the text
Detached from terminal. autoaway_minutes defaults to 15 and autoaway_message to
Idle; set the minutes to 0 to disable idle auto-away. Automatic return from away
occurs only for away state created by these client features, never for manual
/away.

auth accepts none or sasl. With sasl, auth_user is the network account name
and exactly one of password_file, password_gpg_file, or password must be
nonempty. The optional server PASS password independently selects one of
server_password_file, server_password_gpg_file, or server_password. More
than one source for either credential is an error; there is no fallback.
Server PASS is separate from the nickname account. Both authentication
paths require verified TLS. See AUTOMATIC CONNECTION, JOIN, AND
AUTHENTICATION.

Arrows and hjkl always navigate while a text editor is not active. Older
[interface] keymap=original and keymap=vim entries are accepted for migration
but have no effect and are omitted when saving. Other keymap values are
invalid. /keymap is a compatibility command that explains the fixed behavior;
it cannot select a different mapping.

Legacy focus_style=reverse and focus_style=brackets are accepted but ignored,
and saving omits the key. Other values remain invalid. Focus uses bold
text and brackets on the terminal's normal colors; no selector is needed.
history_lines accepts 50 through 5000 retained lines per view, default 500.
The additional per-server 8 MiB history text cap can evict older lines sooner.
Boolean values accept true/false, yes/no, or 1/0 in lowercase. Unknown
sections, unknown keys, invalid values, and oversized values are errors
with a configuration line number where applicable. Most duplicate keys
use the last value; repeated mentions word, ignore mask, and autocommands
command entries add values within their separate limits.

Lines starting with # or ; after leading whitespace are comments. There
are no inline comments: # inside channel=#ircnow is part of the value.
Leading and trailing value whitespace is trimmed, except for autocommands
command= and the two inline
password keys described below. Quotes, backslashes,
environment-variable expansion, ~ expansion, and shell evaluation are not
configuration syntax. Paths are literal; prefer full absolute paths.
Settings Apply and configuration saving reject leading or trailing ASCII
spaces in ordinary text values, including watch phrases and credential-file
paths.
This prevents a saved value from changing when reloaded. Interior spaces
remain valid where the field permits them. Hand-written INI padding keeps
the trimming rule above; quoting or escaping cannot preserve outer spaces.

password and server_password are literal exceptions: every byte after the
first '=' belongs to the password, including leading/trailing spaces,
additional '=', '#', and ';'. Only the line ending is removed. Do not add
quotes, escapes, or an inline comment. Empty means no inline source; a
password consisting of spaces is nonempty. Controls and newlines are invalid.

/save during normal operation generates the whole selected configuration
again, preserving any pending connection choices applied through Settings. It
preserves the supported settings, and replaces hand-written
comments and formatting.
Changes to the file are loaded at the next launch. Keep any explanatory
notes you want to retain outside the generated file.
The command is disabled in --test-mode; edit the file and restart instead.

Generated files have mode 0600. Their final parent directory must belong
to you and have mode 0700. Existing config files must belong to you and
must not be writable by other users. Symlinks in a config or secret path,
including directory components, and '..' path components are refused.
If either inline password or the automatic-command list is nonempty,
including a disabled list, the configuration must be a regular
file owned by you with exactly mode 0600 or 0400. Save always writes 0600.

SAVED SERVER PROFILES

For primary path P, the adjacent P.servers catalog lists up to seven
secondary profiles in the private P.d directory. For the default path,
these are config.ini.servers and config.ini.d beside config.ini. Catalog
syntax is [servers] followed by repeated profile=ID entries. Generated names
use server-<24 lowercase hexadecimal characters>.ini. Manual IDs may contain
1 through 63 ASCII letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, or dots; the first
character must be a letter or digit, and consecutive dots are forbidden.
Directory components and arbitrary paths are not accepted as profile IDs.

Servers > New creates no file. Its first explicit /save or Settings Save
creates a separate mode-0600 profile in the mode-0700 directory and registers
it in the catalog. Subsequent saves update that server's profile. Saving
a secondary never replaces the primary configuration. Startup catalog
updates are locked. Invalid catalog/profile entries produce visible errors;
healthy profiles remain usable.

Close removes a secondary's catalog reference but keeps its profile file.
The primary cannot be closed. --check-config checks the selected primary,
catalog, and referenced profiles without connecting. Connection command-line
overrides apply only to the primary. --no-connect suppresses startup for
all profiles. In test mode, Save is disabled and Close changes runtime only.

AUTOMATIC CONNECTION, JOIN, AND AUTHENTICATION

Settings lets you edit all startup profiles without switching chat. Open a
server from its home screen, enable Auto-connect, set Auto-join channels and
that server's authentication, and Save. Repeat for each desired startup
server. A disabled Auto-connect keeps the saved profile available without
starting it. New server from Settings can add or connect without changing
the active conversation. No other server's credentials are inherited.

An explicitly supplied primary --server starts a connection. Each saved
profile with autoconnect=true connects at startup.
--no-connect overrides startup connection for all profiles. Without automatic
connection, /connect starts the current server; Connect in Servers starts
the selected row. Each server authenticates only with its own configuration.

The channel setting supplies the auto-join list. For automatic account
authentication, configure the account registered with that network:

    [connection]
    tls=true
    auth=sasl
    auth_user=your_registered_account
    password_gpg_file=/home/yourname/.config/vipirc/sasl.gpg

There are three explicit sources for each credential:

    SASL account                  Server PASS
    password_gpg_file              server_password_gpg_file
    password                      server_password
    password_file                 server_password_file

The *_gpg_file settings select encrypted files; the *_file settings select
private plaintext files. password and server_password put plaintext in the
configuration itself. Set only one source in each column and leave the
other two empty. There is no extension detection or fallback to another
source. Settings exposes all sources and masks inline password fields.

Plaintext and decrypted passwords must be one nonempty line, optionally
followed by LF or CRLF, without control bytes. The SASL limit is 1024 bytes;
server PASS is limited to 503 bytes so its IRC line fits the wire limit.
Files of either kind must be regular, owned by you, and mode 0600 or 0400.
Symlinks and '..' path components are refused. Plaintext files can be made
with a text editor; no password is accepted as a vipirc command-line option.

For an inline password, use password= followed immediately by its literal
value, or server_password= for server PASS. Leading/trailing spaces, '#',
';', and '=' are preserved. There is no quote/escape or inline-comment
syntax. A configuration containing an inline password must be mode 0600
or 0400 and owned by you; generated configuration is 0600. It remains
plaintext in that private file and in session configuration while needed
for reconnect or Save.

Encrypted files must contain a single integrity-protected OpenPGP message
and be at most 65536 bytes. GPG is optional; its executable must be named
gpg in PATH and support the fixed options (GnuPG 2.2.20 or newer). For
decryption, vipirc starts it directly after verified TLS, without a shell.
Decryption has a
five-second deadline and bounded memory output, with no plaintext temporary
file. The interface and other sessions continue while it runs. A failed,
locked, invalid, oversized, or timed-out credential stops authentication.

The helper uses --no-options, --batch, --no-tty, --pinentry-mode error,
--no-autostart, and options disabling key retrieval, import, and dirmngr.
It never asks for a GPG passphrase inside the terminal interface. Prepare
the key and unlock the needed agent outside vipirc, for example:

    gpg --output /dev/null --decrypt /absolute/password.gpg

Then run /connect in vipirc. The existing agent must be able to supply the
credential without interaction. No password or GPG passphrase belongs in
the command above. With SSH, the files, PATH, GnuPG home, and agent are in
the environment of the host running vipirc. A different remote session may
have a different agent/cache and require a separate unlock.

--check-config validates source selection and configuration-file privacy
without opening credential sources or starting GPG. --test-mode also never
reads credential files or decrypts; configured inline passwords are parsed
but not used. These modes cannot prove that a real credential is usable.

SASL PLAIN is sent only after successful TLS verification. The server must
support that authentication method. Required authentication failure stops
the connection; channels are not silently joined under an unauthenticated
identity. The client does not register a nickname account on your behalf.
Nickname-service command formats are network-specific; automatic account
authentication in this release uses SASL.

SECURITY AND RESOURCE BOUNDS

TLS verifies the certificate chain and the requested hostname or numeric
address. There is no certificate-verification bypass or silent downgrade.
Plain IRC is available only through an explicit setting; it exposes IRC
traffic to observers on the connection path and cannot use saved secrets.
TLS protects the client-to-server connection, not end-to-end chat privacy.

Incoming IRC data is untrusted. Unsafe control sequences and formatting
are sanitized before display. Input and network buffers are bounded. The
client does not execute received text, launch URLs, run shell commands,
load scripts or plugins, or reply automatically to CTCP requests. Action
messages are displayed as text. DCC SEND offers require explicit per-file
review and acceptance; their direct connections are not encrypted by TLS.

Limits in this release:

    Server sessions per process           8
    Views per server, including builtins  32
    Users stored per channel           4096
    Custom mention strings per server     32
    Ignore masks per server               32
    Queued chat messages per server       64
    Command history entries per server    64
    Command history text per server  64 KiB
    Retained history text per server   8 MiB
    Input Unicode scalars per draft     8192
    Input UTF-8 bytes per draft        16384
    Pending DCC offers, whole workspace    8
    Active DCC transfers, workspace        4
    Retained DCC records, workspace       12

The history cap applies per server, not as a total-process memory cap.
At eight sessions the maximum retained history text is 64 MiB. Server state
is allocated as needed; fewer sessions do not reserve eight full histories.
Libraries, view metadata, user lists, input, and transport use more memory.
History and mentions are not written to disk. Settings and secret files
are local files; other software with your account's privileges can read
them. No client can guarantee safety against every hostile server or a
compromised terminal, operating system, or library.

CREATING ENCRYPTED PASSWORD FILES

Creating a GPG credential: /panel works in both interfaces. Select the server,
choose gpg as the authentication or server-password source, then choose
create.
Create offers an absolute destination in a credentials directory beside the
selected configuration. For the default primary configuration this is:

    ~/.config/vipirc/credentials/account-password.gpg

The server PASS password uses server-password.gpg. Existing names are skipped
with numbered alternatives. The actual absolute path is shown in the panel;
the tilde above is explanatory, not literal configuration syntax.
Enter accepts the offered location and may prepare its private directories
with mode 0700. Viewing the offer creates nothing. A custom destination must
have an existing owned private parent; existing directories are never chmodded.
The destination and local gpg availability are checked before asking for the
key and password. Enter the full 40- or 64-digit hexadecimal fingerprint of
an encryption key already in the local GPG keyring, then enter and repeat
the hidden password. Existing encrypted files remain selectable. Paths entered
in the panel are stored as absolute paths, so another launch directory does
not change their meaning. No key is downloaded or generated, and no plaintext
password file is made.

Only the final Save, Apply, or Connect choice starts encryption and publishes
the explicitly requested new mode-0600 ciphertext. Apply only and Connect once
can create ciphertext while leaving configuration unsaved. Existing files and
symlinks are refused. Each helper has a five-second deadline; the interface
continues processing network events. Encryption failure keeps settings
unapplied and
reports the affected path and reason without secret or helper output. Finish
distinguishes proposed destinations from files already created. A successful
result directs you to /autoauth status for complete paths; a failed save or
partial publication keeps the relevant locations in the scrollable review.
A failed config save can be retried without reencrypting. Cancellation removes only unchanged new files from this attempt;
files already referenced by a saved config are retained. Escape moves back one
question and cancels pending creation; closing setup wipes its hidden inputs.
Offline mode refuses creation before any GPG, keyring, or file access. For
later decryption, unlock the private key outside the application if needed.

TROUBLESHOOTING

No connection: inspect /server for the concrete error. Verify the hostname,
port, network access, and whether the port actually offers TLS. /connect
retries manually. Verify a certificate failure's cause; do not send account
credentials over plain IRC to work around it.

Authentication failure: check the registered account name, the selected
credential source and private permissions, and whether the network supports
SASL PLAIN.
A server PASS password is separate from a nickname-account password.

Credential directory rejected: if this happens at the destination step,
no credential file has been created. The error identifies the directory,
ownership or mode problem. Accept the offered private default or correct the
specific custom directory. Renaming a file does not change its permissions.

Channels not joined: run /autojoin and check the displayed server, registration,
running list and pending list. Required authentication must finish first.
Use /autoauth status to locate the selected credential and distinguish running
authentication from pending settings. Save with /saveconf; for an active
connection, /disconnect then /connect applies those pending settings. Inspect
the server view for rejected JOINs after registration. /autojoin add accepts
one channel per command; a quoted comma-list is not a supported command form.

GPG failure: check gpg --version (2.2.20 or newer), the encrypted file's
ownership/mode/size, and that it contains one integrity-protected message
with a valid one-line password. Unlock it outside vipirc with
gpg --output /dev/null --decrypt /absolute/password.gpg, then retry /connect.
A locked or absent agent cannot open a passphrase prompt inside vipirc.
There is no automatic fallback to a plaintext source.

Nickname rejected or in use: choose another nickname with /nick when the
server permits it, or apply a new nickname in Settings and explicitly Connect
while disconnected. Save that choice to retain it for future launches.

Empty channel view: inspect /server for join refusal, an invite-only or
restricted channel, or authentication requirements. /join requests a join;
it does not override server permissions.

Unusual text widths: use a UTF-8 locale, correct TERM setting, and a terminal
font with the desired glyphs. Unicode width choices can vary by terminal.
Resize the terminal to refresh geometry. Enlarge the window if the sidebar
or input is cramped; the draft and caret are preserved.

Config save refused: use a private directory owned by your account, with
mode 0700, and a normal file path without symbolic links or '..'. /save
does not follow links to another file. Generated configuration is mode 0600.
In --test-mode, saving is deliberately disabled for the whole session.

environment and the BSDs. Requirements are a C11 compiler, POSIX interfaces,

    make check-offline

    make install PREFIX="$HOME/.local"

SECURITY REVIEW AND HARDENING

Common private authentication commands require verified TLS. Logical lines,
split chunks and the send queue are checked; recognized credentials are not
sent over an explicit plaintext connection. Service HELP and ordinary chat
remain available. Unknown credential syntax cannot be reliably detected.

Operational startup refuses mismatched real/effective IDs and disables core
dumps before reading configuration; Linux also disables process dumpability.
The client remains an ordinary single-process application without an OS
sandbox. Use a dedicated unprivileged account for unattended idling.

See doc/SECURITY-REVIEW.txt for the 2026-11-08 review, reproduced defects, exact
validation and remaining platform limitations. make check-security runs the
focused security regressions against local fixtures.

SESSION CONTROL AND DEFAULT INTERFACE

CLOSE A SESSION FROM THE SHELL

List the current jobs. If the IRC worker should survive but its old SSH
terminal is stale, detach only that terminal and then resume it:

  vipirc --sessions
  vipirc --detach-session 1
  vipirc --resume 1

  onekeyirc --sessions
  onekeyirc --detach-session 1
  onekeyirc --resume 1

Use --close-session only when the entire job should end:

  vipirc --close-session 1
  onekeyirc --close-session 1

The number comes from --sessions. It is not a process ID. Each command acts
only within that program's current-user job registry. --detach-session uses
the authenticated private control endpoint to release only the terminal and
waits for the worker to confirm detached state; IRC state remains resumable.
--close-session is deliberately destructive. Closing a job terminates
its entire client session, including all IRC server connections in that job.
It does not mean closing just one channel or one server profile. Unsaved
drafts and in-memory history end with the job. Configuration files remain.

--detach-session=1 and --close-session=1 are also accepted. No interactive terminal or configuration
load is required for this management operation. Do not combine it with
--resume, --sessions, --detach-session, --close-session, connection options or --config. Supported interface
flags can remain in a shell alias but do not change which job is closed.
onekeyirc still rejects -N/--ncurses, including with management commands.

New workers accept verified status, detach and close requests while attached or
detached, while still refusing a second terminal attachment. A close uses
the owned private endpoint, peer-ownership checks and the selected worker's
identity token. The command reports success only after completion is confirmed,
after IRC and transfer cleanup and release of the original job lease.
This confirms application teardown, not an independent observation of OS
process exit. Job numbers may be reused, so inspect the current list before
choosing a number.

The operation has a bounded deadline. If a worker does not answer, cannot
verify its identity, or does not confirm shutdown, the command returns an
error; it does not remove a live endpoint or signal a guessed numeric PID.
A completely wedged process that cannot service its control socket can still
require operating-system intervention after identifying that actual process.
If a request was accepted but completion timed out, shutdown may still finish
later. Recheck --sessions; a nonzero result means completion was not confirmed.

OLDER RUNNING WORKERS

A new executable on disk cannot add this protocol to an already running old
worker. The new client retains older status/attachment compatibility, but
older workers do not implement the close request. They must be quit with
their existing controls or stopped as the correctly identified OS process,
then started with the new executable. An unavailable old job is never
reported as successfully closed merely because its endpoint was removed.

Keep the previous executable until its worker has been stopped if that is
needed for legacy attachment. Job numbers and operating-system PIDs must
not be confused. This release does not deploy to or stop anything on a VPS
automatically.

SSH DISCONNECT RECOVERY

For an already managed background/resumed session, loss of the terminal or
controller now detaches the worker instead of leaving frontend state active
or treating a terminal I/O error as a normal reason to terminate. The paths
cover hangup/error readiness, stdin EOF/EIO, stdout failure, controller EOF,
and direct SIGHUP. The IRC connections and retained client state continue.

In full vipirc, lost-terminal cleanup redirects the worker's standard
descriptors before curses cleanup, so obsolete terminal output cannot hold
that cleanup indefinitely. Ordinary explicit detach still follows its normal
terminal restoration order. A validated external close also redirects worker
output before final cleanup; the foreground controller restores its own tty.

Ordinary curses drawing still uses synchronous terminal output. If a worker
is already blocked rendering to an open, permanently unread terminal, it may
not reach its control poll until the output clears or the terminal closes.
The close command therefore reports timeout honestly instead of claiming a
forced kill. The changes address actual terminal loss; they do not modify
the SSH server's idle-disconnect policy.

An initial ordinary foreground process that has never become a managed
background job retains its existing SIGHUP termination behavior. Start with
--background or use Escape in the minimalist log / the Background command
before relying on a resumable worker.

REMEMBER VIPIRC'S MINIMALIST INTERFACE

In vipirc or vipirc -i, run:

  /set default_interface idle
  /save input

Or add this key to the existing [session] section in the vipirc config:

  [session]
  default_interface=idle

Do not add a second [session] section if one already exists. Keep other
settings, including single_session, in that same section. The setting is
also available in Settings > Interface > Default interface and in vipirc -i's
Application preferences panel. Save the preference explicitly.

The next fresh vipirc launch uses that interface, including --background:

  vipirc                   Use the saved default; ncurses if unset.
  vipirc -i                Use minimalist mode for this launch.
  vipirc --idle            Same as -i.
  vipirc -N                Use ncurses for this launch.
  vipirc --ncurses         Same as -N.

-n and --nick continue to take a nickname. They have not been reassigned.
If both -i and -N occur, the last explicit interface option wins. A command-
line override does not change the saved default, including a later unrelated
Save. Changing the preference does not change the currently attached UI or
reconnect IRC; it selects the next fresh launch.

To restore the saved full interface default:

  /set default_interface ncurses
  /save input

The primary vipirc config owns this application preference. A selected
secondary server does not get to choose a different startup interface.
Existing configs without the new key keep their previous default behavior.

RESUME AND INTERFACE CHOICE

  vipirc --resume 1         Keep that worker's current interface.
  vipirc -i --resume 1      Attach with the minimalist interface.
  vipirc -N --resume 1      Attach with the ncurses interface.

Bare --resume still chooses only a sole verified available detached job.
Several candidates require a number. It does not steal an attached terminal.
An older worker without frontend switching can only retain its own interface.

A saved default applies when a new worker starts; --resume attaches an existing
one. This is why bare --resume retains the worker's current interface instead
of forcing the full screen or reading an unrelated config file.

onekeyirc always uses its minimalist interface. It has the same session close
and hangup fixes, but does not offer a selectable ncurses frontend. -N and
--ncurses are rejected. Its parser can preserve a recognized default_interface
value during unrelated edits; that does not change its fixed runtime mode.

BUILD AND UPGRADE

Build from the extracted source directory using the target host's toolchain:

  ./configure
  make

Stop an older worker cleanly, install the replacement as appropriate for your
setup, confirm --version, and start a fresh worker. The updated source versions
are vipirc 0.7.26 and onekeyirc 0.1.25. Existing configurations remain readable.
Older executables may reject the new key after it has been explicitly saved.


MINIMALIST INPUT VIEW AND WRAPPED CHAT

Opening the minimalist input field keeps recent chat visible above it. Long
messages wrap by terminal columns and the newest visual rows fill the available
area. The input view does not shorten stored or transmitted messages. Older
rows can leave the viewport when the available area fills. Returning to the
ordinary log shows its complete retained records.

A newline after an exactly full editor row uses the same row calculation as
the caret, so the next input line remains in the calculated viewport.

MINIMALIST CATCH-UP AFTER RESUME

The vipirc -i frontend and standalone onekeyirc provide /catchup in a selected
channel or private query. It begins at the first IRC line of your most recent
locally sent composition in that conversation. The anchor is independent per
server and per channel/query. Server/status and mentions views have no sent-chat
anchor.

If the anchor is still in bounded retained memory, no disk log is required. If
it has rolled out during a long absence, persistent_logging must already have
been enabled when that message was sent. Logging remains opt-in because the log
is plaintext. Enable and save it deliberately with:

  /set persistent_logging on
  /save output

After --resume, select each conversation and run /catchup. The reader uses a
stable snapshot of the private capped log instead of loading the whole absence
into permanent chat memory. Up/Down move by row, Page Up/Page Down by page,
Home returns to the sent-message anchor, End moves to the newest snapshot row,
and Escape returns to live chat. New traffic continues to be processed while
the snapshot is open.

Review mode also treats Escape as return-to-editor: at Send this message?,
Escape restores the same Compose/Command draft and caret rather than cancelling
the draft.

This disk-backed /catchup reader belongs to the minimalist frontend in this
release. The regular ncurses conversation view retains its existing bounded
in-memory Page Up/Page Down history.


SECURITY, EFFICIENCY AND STABILITY MAINTENANCE

The 2026-11-15 maintenance pass fixes busy waiting during minimalist message
review and blocked DCC acknowledgements, maintains large rosters incrementally
and indexes disk catch-up pages with bounded memory. See doc/AUDIT-2026-11-15.txt
for reproductions, measurements, validation and environment limitations.
