The nickname and IRC username are different fields. An empty nickname is
prompted at interactive startup. The username defaults from your Unix
account. realname is the descriptive IRC USER field; it need not be your
legal name. channel is a comma-separated auto-join list, without spaces.
An empty channel value leaves you in the server view.

program_messages controls low-priority feedback; queue_notices separately
controls pacing notices. Errors and required confirmations remain visible.
Persistent logging is off by default. When enabled, each saved profile appends
to CONFIG_PATH.log in an owned directory with exact mode 0700. All symlink
components are refused, and the opened file must be owned, single-link,
regular, and exactly mode 0600. A FIFO cannot block the open.

Each log has a 16 MiB limit protected by a nonblocking write lock. Reaching the
limit, encountering an unsafe path, or a write/lock failure stops logging for
that profile and reports an error; live chat continues. Existing data is never
automatically removed. Archive the log, then toggle logging off/on to resume.
Regular files on slow storage can still delay disk I/O. Logs survive exit.
Known outgoing service/credential commands and incoming service replies are
excluded. Unsent drafts and SASL/PASS buffers are not supplied to the logger.
Custom service identities and ordinary chat can still contain secrets.

single_session is false by default. When true, the client refuses creation of a
second background job in its local vipirc namespace. It does not reduce the
eight-server capacity of the one live session; it only makes the local resume
job count singular.

Presence preferences are application-wide. part_message defaults to empty;
quit_message defaults to Client quit. background_away defaults on with the text
Detached from terminal. autoaway_minutes defaults to 15 and autoaway_message to
Idle; set the minutes to 0 to disable idle auto-away. Automatic return from away
occurs only for away state created by these client features, never for manual
/away.

auth accepts none or sasl. With sasl, auth_user is the network account name
and exactly one of password_file, password_gpg_file, or password must be
nonempty. The optional server PASS password independently selects one of
server_password_file, server_password_gpg_file, or server_password. More
than one source for either credential is an error; there is no fallback.
Server PASS is separate from the nickname account. Both authentication
paths require verified TLS. See AUTOMATIC CONNECTION, JOIN, AND
AUTHENTICATION.

Arrows and hjkl always navigate while a text editor is not active. Older
[interface] keymap=original and keymap=vim entries are accepted for migration
but have no effect and are omitted when saving. Other keymap values are
invalid. /keymap is a compatibility command that explains the fixed behavior;
it cannot select a different mapping.

Legacy focus_style=reverse and focus_style=brackets are accepted but ignored,
and saving omits the key. Other values remain invalid. Focus uses bold
text and brackets on the terminal's normal colors; no selector is needed.
history_lines accepts 50 through 5000 retained lines per view, default 500.
The additional per-server 8 MiB history text cap can evict older lines sooner.
Boolean values accept true/false, yes/no, or 1/0 in lowercase. Unknown
sections, unknown keys, invalid values, and oversized values are errors
with a configuration line number where applicable. Most duplicate keys
use the last value; repeated mentions word, ignore mask, and autocommands
command entries add values within their separate limits.

Lines starting with # or ; after leading whitespace are comments. There
are no inline comments: # inside channel=#ircnow is part of the value.
Leading and trailing value whitespace is trimmed, except for autocommands
command= and the two inline
password keys described below. Quotes, backslashes,
environment-variable expansion, ~ expansion, and shell evaluation are not
configuration syntax. Paths are literal; prefer full absolute paths.
Settings Apply and configuration saving reject leading or trailing ASCII
spaces in ordinary text values, including watch phrases and credential-file
paths.
This prevents a saved value from changing when reloaded. Interior spaces
remain valid where the field permits them. Hand-written INI padding keeps
the trimming rule above; quoting or escaping cannot preserve outer spaces.

password and server_password are literal exceptions: every byte after the
first '=' belongs to the password, including leading/trailing spaces,
additional '=', '#', and ';'. Only the line ending is removed. Do not add
quotes, escapes, or an inline comment. Empty means no inline source; a
password consisting of spaces is nonempty. Controls and newlines are invalid.

/save during normal operation generates the whole selected configuration
again, preserving any pending connection choices applied through Settings. It
preserves the supported settings, and replaces hand-written
comments and formatting.
Changes to the file are loaded at the next launch. Keep any explanatory
notes you want to retain outside the generated file.
The command is disabled in --test-mode; edit the file and restart instead.

Generated files have mode 0600. Their final parent directory must belong
to you and have mode 0700. Existing config files must belong to you and
must not be writable by other users. Symlinks in a config or secret path,
including directory components, and '..' path components are refused.
If either inline password or the automatic-command list is nonempty,
including a disabled list, the configuration must be a regular
file owned by you with exactly mode 0600 or 0400. Save always writes 0600.

SAVED SERVER PROFILES

For primary path P, the adjacent P.servers catalog lists up to seven
secondary profiles in the private P.d directory. For the default path,
these are config.ini.servers and config.ini.d beside config.ini. Catalog
syntax is [servers] followed by repeated profile=ID entries. Generated names
use server-<24 lowercase hexadecimal characters>.ini. Manual IDs may contain
1 through 63 ASCII letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, or dots; the first
character must be a letter or digit, and consecutive dots are forbidden.
Directory components and arbitrary paths are not accepted as profile IDs.

Servers > New creates no file. Its first explicit /save or Settings Save
creates a separate mode-0600 profile in the mode-0700 directory and registers
it in the catalog. Subsequent saves update that server's profile. Saving
a secondary never replaces the primary configuration. Startup catalog
updates are locked. Invalid catalog/profile entries produce visible errors;
healthy profiles remain usable.

Close removes a secondary's catalog reference but keeps its profile file.
The primary cannot be closed. --check-config checks the selected primary,
catalog, and referenced profiles without connecting. Connection command-line
overrides apply only to the primary. --no-connect suppresses startup for
all profiles. In test mode, Save is disabled and Close changes runtime only.

AUTOMATIC CONNECTION, JOIN, AND AUTHENTICATION

Settings lets you edit all startup profiles without switching chat. Open a
server from its home screen, enable Auto-connect, set Auto-join channels and
that server's authentication, and Save. Repeat for each desired startup
server. A disabled Auto-connect keeps the saved profile available without
starting it. New server from Settings can add or connect without changing
the active conversation. No other server's credentials are inherited.

An explicitly supplied primary --server starts a connection. Each saved
profile with autoconnect=true connects at startup.
--no-connect overrides startup connection for all profiles. Without automatic
connection, /connect starts the current server; Connect in Servers starts
the selected row. Each server authenticates only with its own configuration.

The channel setting supplies the auto-join list. For automatic account
authentication, configure the account registered with that network:

    [connection]
    tls=true
    auth=sasl
    auth_user=your_registered_account
    password_gpg_file=/home/yourname/.config/vipirc/sasl.gpg

There are three explicit sources for each credential:

    SASL account                  Server PASS
    password_gpg_file              server_password_gpg_file
    password                      server_password
    password_file                 server_password_file

The *_gpg_file settings select encrypted files; the *_file settings select
private plaintext files. password and server_password put plaintext in the
configuration itself. Set only one source in each column and leave the
other two empty. There is no extension detection or fallback to another
source. Settings exposes all sources and masks inline password fields.

Plaintext and decrypted passwords must be one nonempty line, optionally
followed by LF or CRLF, without control bytes. The SASL limit is 1024 bytes;
server PASS is limited to 503 bytes so its IRC line fits the wire limit.
Files of either kind must be regular, owned by you, and mode 0600 or 0400.
Symlinks and '..' path components are refused. Plaintext files can be made
with a text editor; no password is accepted as a vipirc command-line option.

For an inline password, use password= followed immediately by its literal
value, or server_password= for server PASS. Leading/trailing spaces, '#',
';', and '=' are preserved. There is no quote/escape or inline-comment
syntax. A configuration containing an inline password must be mode 0600
or 0400 and owned by you; generated configuration is 0600. It remains
plaintext in that private file and in session configuration while needed
for reconnect or Save.

Encrypted files must contain a single integrity-protected OpenPGP message
and be at most 65536 bytes. GPG is optional; its executable must be named
gpg in PATH and support the fixed options (GnuPG 2.2.20 or newer). For
decryption, vipirc starts it directly after verified TLS, without a shell.
Decryption has a
five-second deadline and bounded memory output, with no plaintext temporary
file. The interface and other sessions continue while it runs. A failed,
locked, invalid, oversized, or timed-out credential stops authentication.

The helper uses --no-options, --batch, --no-tty, --pinentry-mode error,
--no-autostart, and options disabling key retrieval, import, and dirmngr.
It never asks for a GPG passphrase inside the terminal interface. Prepare
the key and unlock the needed agent outside vipirc, for example:

    gpg --output /dev/null --decrypt /absolute/password.gpg

Then run /connect in vipirc. The existing agent must be able to supply the
credential without interaction. No password or GPG passphrase belongs in
the command above. With SSH, the files, PATH, GnuPG home, and agent are in
the environment of the host running vipirc. A different remote session may
have a different agent/cache and require a separate unlock.

--check-config validates source selection and configuration-file privacy
without opening credential sources or starting GPG. --test-mode also never
reads credential files or decrypts; configured inline passwords are parsed
but not used. These modes cannot prove that a real credential is usable.

SASL PLAIN is sent only after successful TLS verification. The server must
support that authentication method. Required authentication failure stops
the connection; channels are not silently joined under an unauthenticated
identity. The client does not register a nickname account on your behalf.
Nickname-service command formats are network-specific; automatic account
authentication in this release uses SASL.

SECURITY AND RESOURCE BOUNDS

TLS verifies the certificate chain and the requested hostname or numeric
address. There is no certificate-verification bypass or silent downgrade.
Plain IRC is available only through an explicit setting; it exposes IRC
traffic to observers on the connection path and cannot use saved secrets.
TLS protects the client-to-server connection, not end-to-end chat privacy.

Incoming IRC data is untrusted. Unsafe control sequences and formatting
are sanitized before display. Input and network buffers are bounded. The
client does not execute received text, launch URLs, run shell commands,
load scripts or plugins, or reply automatically to CTCP requests. Action
messages are displayed as text. DCC SEND offers require explicit per-file
review and acceptance; their direct connections are not encrypted by TLS.

Limits in this release:

    Server sessions per process           8
    Views per server, including builtins  32
    Users stored per channel           4096
    Custom mention strings per server     32
    Ignore masks per server               32
    Queued chat messages per server       64
    Command history entries per server    64
    Command history text per server  64 KiB
    Retained history text per server   8 MiB
    Input Unicode scalars per draft     8192
    Input UTF-8 bytes per draft        16384
    Pending DCC offers, whole workspace    8
    Active DCC transfers, workspace        4
    Retained DCC records, workspace       12

The history cap applies per server, not as a total-process memory cap.
At eight sessions the maximum retained history text is 64 MiB. Server state
is allocated as needed; fewer sessions do not reserve eight full histories.
Libraries, view metadata, user lists, input, and transport use more memory.
History and mentions are not written to disk. Settings and secret files
are local files; other software with your account's privileges can read
them. No client can guarantee safety against every hostile server or a
compromised terminal, operating system, or library.

CREATING ENCRYPTED PASSWORD FILES

Creating a GPG credential: /panel works in both interfaces. Select the server,
choose gpg as the authentication or server-password source, then choose
create.
Create offers an absolute destination in a credentials directory beside the
selected configuration. For the default primary configuration this is:

    ~/.config/vipirc/credentials/account-password.gpg

The server PASS password uses server-password.gpg. Existing names are skipped
with numbered alternatives. The actual absolute path is shown in the panel;
the tilde above is explanatory, not literal configuration syntax.
Enter accepts the offered location and may prepare its private directories
with mode 0700. Viewing the offer creates nothing. A custom destination must
have an existing owned private parent; existing directories are never chmodded.
The destination and local gpg availability are checked before asking for the
key and password. Enter the full 40- or 64-digit hexadecimal fingerprint of
an encryption key already in the local GPG keyring, then enter and repeat
the hidden password. Existing encrypted files remain selectable. Paths entered
in the panel are stored as absolute paths, so another launch directory does
not change their meaning. No key is downloaded or generated, and no plaintext
password file is made.

Only the final Save, Apply, or Connect choice starts encryption and publishes
the explicitly requested new mode-0600 ciphertext. Apply only and Connect once
can create ciphertext while leaving configuration unsaved. Existing files and
symlinks are refused. Each helper has a five-second deadline; the interface
continues processing network events. Encryption failure keeps settings
unapplied and
reports the affected path and reason without secret or helper output. Finish
distinguishes proposed destinations from files already created. A successful
result directs you to /autoauth status for complete paths; a failed save or
partial publication keeps the relevant locations in the scrollable review.
A failed config save can be retried without reencrypting. Cancellation removes only unchanged new files from this attempt;
files already referenced by a saved config are retained. Escape moves back one
question and cancels pending creation; closing setup wipes its hidden inputs.
Offline mode refuses creation before any GPG, keyring, or file access. For
later decryption, unlock the private key outside the application if needed.

TROUBLESHOOTING

No connection: inspect /server for the concrete error. Verify the hostname,
port, network access, and whether the port actually offers TLS. /connect
retries manually. Verify a certificate failure's cause; do not send account
credentials over plain IRC to work around it.

Authentication failure: check the registered account name, the selected
credential source and private permissions, and whether the network supports
SASL PLAIN.
A server PASS password is separate from a nickname-account password.

Credential directory rejected: if this happens at the destination step,
no credential file has been created. The error identifies the directory,
ownership or mode problem. Accept the offered private default or correct the
specific custom directory. Renaming a file does not change its permissions.

Channels not joined: run /autojoin and check the displayed server, registration,
running list and pending list. Required authentication must finish first.
Use /autoauth status to locate the selected credential and distinguish running
authentication from pending settings. Save with /saveconf; for an active
connection, /disconnect then /connect applies those pending settings. Inspect
the server view for rejected JOINs after registration. /autojoin add accepts
one channel per command; a quoted comma-list is not a supported command form.

GPG failure: check gpg --version (2.2.20 or newer), the encrypted file's
ownership/mode/size, and that it contains one integrity-protected message
with a valid one-line password. Unlock it outside vipirc with
gpg --output /dev/null --decrypt /absolute/password.gpg, then retry /connect.
A locked or absent agent cannot open a passphrase prompt inside vipirc.
There is no automatic fallback to a plaintext source.

Nickname rejected or in use: choose another nickname with /nick when the
server permits it, or apply a new nickname in Settings and explicitly Connect
while disconnected. Save that choice to retain it for future launches.

Empty channel view: inspect /server for join refusal, an invite-only or
restricted channel, or authentication requirements. /join requests a join;
it does not override server permissions.

Unusual text widths: use a UTF-8 locale, correct TERM setting, and a terminal
font with the desired glyphs. Unicode width choices can vary by terminal.
Resize the terminal to refresh geometry. Enlarge the window if the sidebar
or input is cramped; the draft and caret are preserved.

Config save refused: use a private directory owned by your account, with
mode 0700, and a normal file path without symbolic links or '..'. /save
does not follow links to another file. Generated configuration is mode 0600.
In --test-mode, saving is deliberately disabled for the whole session.

SESSION CONTROL AND DEFAULT INTERFACE

CLOSE A SESSION FROM THE SHELL

List the current jobs. If the IRC worker should survive but its old SSH
terminal is stale, detach only that terminal and then resume it:

  vipirc --sessions
  vipirc --detach-session 1
  vipirc --resume 1

  onekeyirc --sessions
  onekeyirc --detach-session 1
  onekeyirc --resume 1

Use --close-session only when the entire job should end:

  vipirc --close-session 1
  onekeyirc --close-session 1

The number comes from --sessions. It is not a process ID. Each command acts
only within that program's current-user job registry. --detach-session uses
the authenticated private control endpoint to release only the terminal and
waits for the worker to confirm detached state; IRC state remains resumable.
--close-session is deliberately destructive. Closing a job terminates
its entire client session, including all IRC server connections in that job.
It does not mean closing just one channel or one server profile. Unsaved
drafts and in-memory history end with the job. Configuration files remain.

--detach-session=1 and --close-session=1 are also accepted. No interactive terminal or configuration
load is required for this management operation. Do not combine it with
--resume, --sessions, --detach-session, --close-session, connection options or --config. Supported interface
flags can remain in a shell alias but do not change which job is closed.
onekeyirc still rejects -N/--ncurses, including with management commands.

New workers accept verified status, detach and close requests while attached or
detached, while still refusing a second terminal attachment. A close uses
the owned private endpoint, peer-ownership checks and the selected worker's
identity token. The command reports success only after completion is confirmed,
after IRC and transfer cleanup and release of the original job lease.
This confirms application teardown, not an independent observation of OS
process exit. Job numbers may be reused, so inspect the current list before
choosing a number.

The operation has a bounded deadline. If a worker does not answer, cannot
verify its identity, or does not confirm shutdown, the command returns an
error; it does not remove a live endpoint or signal a guessed numeric PID.
A completely wedged process that cannot service its control socket can still
require operating-system intervention after identifying that actual process.
If a request was accepted but completion timed out, shutdown may still finish
later. Recheck --sessions; a nonzero result means completion was not confirmed.

OLDER RUNNING WORKERS

A new executable on disk cannot add this protocol to an already running old
worker. The new client retains older status/attachment compatibility, but
older workers do not implement the close request. They must be quit with
their existing controls or stopped as the correctly identified OS process,
then started with the new executable. An unavailable old job is never
reported as successfully closed merely because its endpoint was removed.

Keep the previous executable until its worker has been stopped if that is
needed for legacy attachment. Job numbers and operating-system PIDs must
not be confused. This release does not deploy to or stop anything on a VPS
automatically.

SSH DISCONNECT RECOVERY

For an already managed background/resumed session, loss of the terminal or
controller now detaches the worker instead of leaving frontend state active
or treating a terminal I/O error as a normal reason to terminate. The paths
cover hangup/error readiness, stdin EOF/EIO, stdout failure, controller EOF,
and direct SIGHUP. The IRC connections and retained client state continue.

In full vipirc, lost-terminal cleanup redirects the worker's standard
descriptors before curses cleanup, so obsolete terminal output cannot hold
that cleanup indefinitely. Ordinary explicit detach still follows its normal
terminal restoration order. A validated external close also redirects worker
output before final cleanup; the foreground controller restores its own tty.

Ordinary curses drawing still uses synchronous terminal output. If a worker
is already blocked rendering to an open, permanently unread terminal, it may
not reach its control poll until the output clears or the terminal closes.
The close command therefore reports timeout honestly instead of claiming a
forced kill. The changes address actual terminal loss; they do not modify
the SSH server's idle-disconnect policy.

An initial ordinary foreground process that has never become a managed
background job retains its existing SIGHUP termination behavior. Start with
--background or use Escape in the minimalist log / the Background command
before relying on a resumable worker.

REMEMBER VIPIRC'S MINIMALIST INTERFACE

In vipirc or vipirc -i, run:

  /set default_interface idle
  /save input

Or add this key to the existing [session] section in the vipirc config:

  [session]
  default_interface=idle

Do not add a second [session] section if one already exists. Keep other
settings, including single_session, in that same section. The setting is
also available in Settings > Interface > Default interface and in vipirc -i's
Application preferences panel. Save the preference explicitly.

The next fresh vipirc launch uses that interface, including --background:

  vipirc                   Use the saved default; ncurses if unset.
  vipirc -i                Use minimalist mode for this launch.
  vipirc --idle            Same as -i.
  vipirc -N                Use ncurses for this launch.
  vipirc --ncurses         Same as -N.

-n and --nick continue to take a nickname. They have not been reassigned.
If both -i and -N occur, the last explicit interface option wins. A command-
line override does not change the saved default, including a later unrelated
Save. Changing the preference does not change the currently attached UI or
reconnect IRC; it selects the next fresh launch.

To restore the saved full interface default:

  /set default_interface ncurses
  /save input

The primary vipirc config owns this application preference. A selected
secondary server does not get to choose a different startup interface.
Existing configs without the new key keep their previous default behavior.

RESUME AND INTERFACE CHOICE

  vipirc --resume 1         Keep that worker's current interface.
  vipirc -i --resume 1      Attach with the minimalist interface.
  vipirc -N --resume 1      Attach with the ncurses interface.

Bare --resume still chooses only a sole verified available detached job.
Several candidates require a number. It does not steal an attached terminal.
An older worker without frontend switching can only retain its own interface.

A saved default applies when a new worker starts; --resume attaches an existing
one. This is why bare --resume retains the worker's current interface instead
of forcing the full screen or reading an unrelated config file.

onekeyirc always uses its minimalist interface. It has the same session close
and hangup fixes, but does not offer a selectable ncurses frontend. -N and
--ncurses are rejected. Its parser can preserve a recognized default_interface
value during unrelated edits; that does not change its fixed runtime mode.

Build from the extracted source directory using the target host's toolchain:

  ./configure
  make

Stop an older worker cleanly, install the replacement as appropriate for your
setup, confirm --version, and start a fresh worker. The updated source versions
are vipirc 0.7.25 and onekeyirc 0.1.24. Existing configurations remain readable.
Older executables may reject the new key after it has been explicitly saved.


MINIMALIST INPUT VIEW AND WRAPPED CHAT

Opening the minimalist input field keeps recent chat visible above it. Long
messages wrap by terminal columns and the newest visual rows fill the available
area. The input view does not shorten stored or transmitted messages. Older
rows can leave the viewport when the available area fills. Returning to the
ordinary log shows its complete retained records.

A newline after an exactly full editor row uses the same row calculation as
the caret, so the next input line remains in the calculated viewport.

MINIMALIST CATCH-UP AFTER RESUME

The vipirc -i frontend and standalone onekeyirc provide /catchup in a selected
channel or private query. It begins at the first IRC line of your most recent
locally sent composition in that conversation. The anchor is independent per
server and per channel/query. Server/status and mentions views have no sent-chat
anchor.

If the anchor is still in bounded retained memory, no disk log is required. If
it has rolled out during a long absence, persistent_logging must already have
been enabled when that message was sent. Logging remains opt-in because the log
is plaintext. Enable and save it deliberately with:

  /set persistent_logging on
  /save output

After --resume, select each conversation and run /catchup. The reader uses a
stable snapshot of the private capped log instead of loading the whole absence
into permanent chat memory. Up/Down move by row, Page Up/Page Down by page,
Home returns to the sent-message anchor, End moves to the newest snapshot row,
and Escape returns to live chat. New traffic continues to be processed while
the snapshot is open.

Review mode also treats Escape as return-to-editor: at Send this message?,
Escape restores the same Compose/Command draft and caret rather than cancelling
the draft.

This disk-backed /catchup reader belongs to the minimalist frontend in this
release. The regular ncurses conversation view retains its existing bounded
in-memory Page Up/Page Down history.
